nutrients.name: Vitamin C

whatItDoes.text: A water-soluble antioxidant that helps protect cells from free-radical damage. Needed to make collagen, a protein required for wound healing. Improves absorption of iron from plant-based foods, and helps the immune system work properly.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: Vitamin C and the common cold: a Cochrane systematic review (Hemila & Chalker, 2013) found regular vitamin C supplementation did not reduce the risk of catching a cold in the general population, but did modestly shorten how long a cold lasted (about 8% shorter in adults, 18% shorter in children) once someone was already sick. Separately, people under heavy physical stress (elite athletes, soldiers training in Arctic conditions) who took vitamin C supplements had around 50% fewer colds than those who did not - a specific finding for people under extreme physical stress, not a general population effect. This is a modest, honest picture - vitamin C is not a reliable way to avoid catching a cold for most people.
whatItDoes.label: open question

whatItDoes.text: Vitamin C and cataracts: a 7-year follow-up study found vitamin C supplements gave no benefit in preventing cataracts, despite earlier hopes based on its antioxidant properties. Worth knowing so this card does not overstate what vitamin C can do for eye health.
whatItDoes.label: open question

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: NIH's US adult-male figure (90 mg/day) is notably higher than ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian men (80 mg/day). Both shown rather than merged into one number.

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: Same pattern as for men - NIH's figure is notably higher than ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian women.

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: add 35 mg/day to the figure for their age/group above
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Vitamin C is not a nutrient vegans are specifically short on - unlike most of this project's other nutrient cards, this one exists for its cross-reference value (it meaningfully boosts iron absorption and supports immune function - see this project's iron and immune-function cards) rather than because vegans are at particular risk of falling short on it. NIH's own food-source list is almost entirely fruits and vegetables (citrus fruits and juices, red and green pepper, kiwifruit, broccoli, strawberries, cantaloupe, baked potatoes, tomatoes) - foods that feature heavily in an ordinary varied vegan diet, likely more so than in a typical diet with less fruit and vegetable intake. This card should not read as 'another nutrient vegans need to watch' - it isn't one.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Approximate vitamin C content of some everyday foods: orange, 1 medium, about 70 mg; orange juice, 3/4 cup, about 75 mg; grapefruit, half, about 44 mg; grapefruit juice, 3/4 cup, about 60 mg; strawberries, 1 cup, about 82 mg; papaya, 1, about 94 mg; tomato, 1 medium, about 23 mg; red bell pepper, half cup raw, about 141 mg; broccoli, steamed, half cup, about 62 mg; cauliflower, boiled, half cup, about 27 mg; potato, 1 medium baked, about 26 mg.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: The American Cancer Society recommends meeting vitamin C needs by increasing healthy foods in the diet rather than relying on a dietary supplement - studies on vitamin C supplements and cancer risk specifically have given mixed results. Separately, the American Heart Association recommends increasing vitamin C (and other vitamins and minerals) through more fresh vegetables rather than through supplementation for cardiovascular health, and notes vitamin C does not reduce blood cholesterol levels. Both reinforce this card's existing food-first framing.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Vitamin C is considered safe for women to take during pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and passes into breast milk.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A separate general food-health reference independently gives the same RDA figures already in this card (90 mg men, 75 mg women) and names a similar vegan-compatible food list (citrus fruits and juices, melons, berries, peppers, broccoli, potatoes and many other fruits and vegetables) - a second, independent confirmation of this card's existing figures and food sources.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: This is this card's main practical job: vitamin C meaningfully improves how much nonheme (plant) iron the body absorbs when eaten in the same meal - NIH states this directly as one of vitamin C's functions. This is the anchor source for this project's existing iron-card advice to pair iron-rich plant foods (lentils, beans, spinach) with a vitamin C food (citrus, peppers, tomatoes, broccoli) at the same meal - see the iron nutrient card for the food-pairing detail itself, not repeated here.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Vitamin C content is reduced by prolonged storage and by cooking - steaming or microwaving loses less than boiling. Many of the best vitamin C sources (fruit, salad vegetables) are usually eaten raw anyway, which avoids the issue.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Ordinary high intake (well above the official upper limit of 2,000 mg/day for adults, usually from supplements rather than food) can cause diarrhoea, nausea and stomach cramps.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: People with haemochromatosis (a condition that causes the body to store too much iron) are a specific exception to vitamin C's general food-tier/green status: because vitamin C increases iron absorption, high-dose vitamin C could worsen their existing iron overload and damage body tissues. This is a real, named caution for that specific condition, not a general population risk - NIH separately notes that in healthy people, vitamin C's iron-absorption-boosting effect is only a theoretical concern, not an actual one. Vitamin C supplementation is also specifically flagged as something to avoid in a few other blood disorders - thalassemia, G6PD deficiency and sickle cell disease - because of similar iron-handling or oxidative-stress concerns; anyone with one of these conditions should check with their doctor before taking a vitamin C supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: High vitamin C intake can raise urinary oxalate and uric acid, which could contribute to kidney stone formation, especially in people with an existing kidney/renal disorder - NIH's own health-professional guidance is careful here: studies on this have had conflicting results, it is not generally considered a risk in healthy people, and the best evidence for an actual contribution is specifically in people who already have hyperoxaluria (an existing high-oxalate condition). Worth knowing rather than worth fearing for most readers - see this project's kidney-health card for oxalate detail generally.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Large daily doses of vitamin C may interfere with the body's absorption of vitamin B12 - worth knowing for vegans specifically, since a reliable B12 source (supplement or fortified food) is already essential on a vegan diet; taking a large vitamin C dose at the same time as a B12 source is not an ideal pairing.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Generally, parents should have few concerns about children getting too much or too little vitamin C from food. Children under age one should not be given a vitamin C dietary supplement specifically - their needs should be met through the foods they eat.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: A blood test for vitamin C status usually reports plasma ascorbic acid; a level below roughly 23 micromol/L (0.4 mg/dL) indicates hypovitaminosis C. This is mainly a research/clinical tool - true clinically visible vitamin C deficiency is rarely seen outside hospital patients with high inflammation or oxidative stress (such as major surgery, burns or sepsis), not something a person would typically have tested as part of routine care.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Eat citrus fruit, peppers, tomatoes or other vitamin-C-rich produce alongside your iron-rich meals (dal, beans, spinach) - that pairing is this nutrient's single most useful everyday job for a vegan diet.
gaps: No source found for a vitamin-C-specific blood test reference range tied to a specific symptom threshold beyond the general hypovitaminosis cutoff above - vitamin C status is not typically checked with a routine standalone blood test the way iron or B12 are.

The food-content figures sourced from book-encyclopedia-of-diets (a pre-2015 reference encyclopedia, author unstated) have not been independently cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central - flagged for a recheck before being treated as precise rather than approximate.

foods.name: Agar (agar-agar)
foods.notes: Basic entry. Figures are real USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy) values for raw agar (fdc_id 169280, per 100 g), not estimated. Agar-agar is used in India mainly as a vegan gelatin substitute for desserts (China grass), bought dried in small amounts rather than eaten as a vegetable; included here for food-group completeness per BRIEF.md's Completeness rules, not as a nutrient-dense staple - a typical serving used in cooking is a small fraction of 100 g. Vitamin A and vitamin K are present in USDA's record but deliberately left off: the vitamin K value is phylloquinone (vitamin K1), not the vitamin K2 (menaquinone) this project tracks separately, and vitamin A, RAE is 0 for this food. USDA's record carries a tiny EPA value (0.008 g) but no ALA (the plant omega-3 this project tracks) and no iodine value (checked directly - both fields are empty for ALA/iodine), so omega-3 and iodine are left off rather than estimated.
foods.localNameStatus: No local name proposed yet - though sold in India as 'China grass', that is a product/brand-style name, not a vernacular translation, so no candidate is proposed here without the owner's confirmation.

healthTopics.name: Anaemia
healthTopics.whyItMatters: SAMPLE: anaemia from low iron is a common concern on any diet, including vegan diets, especially for women.
healthTopics.whatToFocusOn: SAMPLE: enough iron-rich plant foods, eaten with vitamin C, and tea or coffee kept away from meals.
healthTopics.pairings: SAMPLE: vitamin C foods such as amla, lemon or tomato alongside iron-rich foods; tea and coffee at least an hour away from meals.
healthTopics.preparation: SAMPLE: soaking and sprouting legumes reduces phytates that block iron absorption.
healthTopics.samplePlate: SAMPLE: rajma-chawal with a side of lemon and tomato salad.
healthTopics.redFlags: SAMPLE: see a doctor if you feel constantly tired, breathless, dizzy or notice pale skin or nails — do not self-treat anaemia.
healthTopics.whatFoodCannotDo: SAMPLE: food alone cannot fix anaemia caused by heavy bleeding or an absorption problem; that needs medical attention.
healthTopics.lifestyleLinks: SAMPLE: placeholder — regular meals and good sleep support overall recovery.

healthTopics.name: Bones

healthTopics.whatToFocusOn: SAMPLE: a steady calcium intake across the day, sensible sunlight, and regular activity.
healthTopics.pairings: SAMPLE: calcium is absorbed better when spread across meals rather than in one large dose.

healthTopics.redFlags: SAMPLE: see a doctor if you have a fracture from a minor fall, or a family history of early osteoporosis.
healthTopics.whatFoodCannotDo: SAMPLE: food cannot replace sunlight for vitamin D or replace weight-bearing exercise for bone strength.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A well-planned vegan diet that covers zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D well supports normal, healthy skin and hair - this is about supporting that normal function through nutrient adequacy, not about a vegan diet making hair or skin better than anyone else's. See this project's own zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D nutrient cards for daily targets and food sources; this card exists to connect them to the skin/hair reason they matter, not to repeat them.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A poorly planned or crash vegan diet - not veganism itself - is the real driver of hair thinning and dull skin. The same honesty pattern this project uses for mood and immune function applies here: a sudden, large calorie cut, cutting out whole food groups without replacing them, or simply not planning what used to come from animal foods (protein, zinc, iron) is what causes trouble, not the decision to eat plant-based. This card should never read as 'going vegan causes hair loss' - that is not what the evidence behind it says.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: One genuine, dermatology-sourced incidental benefit worth naming calmly, not oversold: the American Academy of Dermatology's own review of the evidence links cow's milk specifically - not dairy broadly - to higher rates of acne in several large cohort studies (for example, women drinking 2 or more glasses of skim milk a day were 44% more likely to have acne in one 47,355-woman study). The AAD states plainly that no such link has been found for yogurt or cheese, so this is a milk-specific finding, not a reason to think 'dairy-free' alone clears skin - a vegan diet simply avoids milk by default, which happens to line up with this specific piece of evidence. The mechanism is still unclear (a theory involves hormones in milk triggering inflammation), and the AAD itself is careful not to claim settled causation.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Guggul, a traditional Ayurvedic gum-resin herb some readers may take separately as a supplement, has a real but genuinely disputed research link to acne. A small 1994 Indian trial found oral gugulipid reduced inflammatory acne lesions about as well as the antibiotic tetracycline, especially in people with oily skin - but a US consumer reference rates this "Possibly Effective" largely on that one small trial, while a cancer-centre clinical database states plainly that evidence is lacking for guggul alone on acne. This card treats it as an open question, not a confirmed acne treatment. See this project's own Guggul herb card for full detail, including its thyroid and bleeding-risk cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Covering zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D well is the main lever - see this project's own nutrient cards for daily targets, vegan food sources and absorption tips for each.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: A real gap worth naming honestly: biotin also comes up often in hair/skin conversations, but this project does not yet have a dedicated biotin nutrient card, so it cannot be given the same daily-target/food-source treatment zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D get here. This is less urgent than it might sound - a dermatology review of the evidence states that average dietary biotin intake is adequate in a normal diet, biotin deficiency is rare, and 'severe biotin deficiency in healthy individuals eating a normal diet has never been reported.' The same review and a companion dermatology-journal review both conclude that biotin supplementation for hair/skin/nails is not well supported by large-scale evidence outside an actual deficiency state - so this gap is a documentation one, not a sign that vegans specifically need to worry about biotin.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Zinc specifically: alopecia (hair loss) is a well-known sign of an established zinc deficiency, with hair regrowth occurring once the deficiency is corrected - this is the clearest, most defensible zinc-hair link, and it is about avoiding deficiency, not about more zinc meaning more hair for someone already getting enough. The same review notes that evidence linking zinc levels to the more common, everyday forms of hair thinning (in people who are not zinc-deficient) is inconsistent across studies - so this card does not claim extra zinc will thicken hair in someone whose zinc status is already adequate.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Crash or heavily restrictive vegan transitions - suddenly cutting calories, dropping whole food groups, or not deliberately replacing the protein, zinc and iron that used to come from animal foods - are the real, documented risk factor for hair thinning and dull skin, not veganism as such. A gradual, planned transition that keeps calories and these nutrients adequate does not carry the same risk.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Phytates in beans and grains reduce how much zinc the body absorbs from them - this project's zinc card already covers this and the soaking/sprouting/fermenting tip that helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Do not expect biotin or zinc supplements, taken on top of an already-adequate diet, to meaningfully improve hair or skin - the dermatology evidence for supplementing beyond normal dietary adequacy is weak, and more is not simply better here.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting or fermenting beans and grains before cooking lowers their phytate content and can improve zinc absorption.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Ground flaxseed absorbs better for its omega-3 content than whole flaxseed, as already noted in this project's omega-3 card.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) and tree nuts (walnuts), both named above, are recognised allergens; chickpeas, lentils, black gram, flaxseed or sunflower seeds are reasonable substitutes for zinc/iron/protein/omega-3 if either affects you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with masoor dal or chana curry, a side of tofu or tempeh, rice or roti with a spoon of ground flaxseed stirred in, and a fortified soy milk alongside - covering zinc, iron, protein and omega-3 together, with fortified soy milk as one route to vitamin D if the label confirms it.

redFlags.text: This card is about diet supporting normal skin and hair through nutrient adequacy - it cannot diagnose or treat a dermatological condition. See a doctor or dermatologist for sudden or patchy hair loss, a scalp that is painful, itchy, flaking or inflamed, or a skin condition that is worsening or not responding to ordinary skin care.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Hair thinning and skin changes can also come from causes unrelated to diet - thyroid conditions, hormonal changes, certain medicines, stress, or skin conditions like alopecia areata, eczema or psoriasis. If diet changes alone don't explain what you're seeing, or nutrient levels have already been checked and look fine, see a doctor rather than assuming it's a dietary gap.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support the normal nutrient adequacy healthy skin and hair depend on - but no food, diet or supplement guarantees faster or thicker hair growth beyond that normal baseline, treats an underlying dermatological or medical condition, or substitutes for a dermatologist's diagnosis and care.

myths.claim: Vegans always need B12 injections, tablets are not enough.
myths.evidence: SAMPLE: for most people, a regular oral vegan B12 supplement raises blood B12 levels effectively; injections are usually only needed for a diagnosed absorption problem.

myths.claim: You cannot build or keep muscle without eating meat.
myths.evidence: SAMPLE: a varied vegan diet with enough total protein from legumes, soy foods, grains and nuts supports muscle building and maintenance just as well, given enough total intake.

myths.claim: Spinach is one of the best vegan sources of iron.
myths.evidence: SAMPLE: spinach does contain iron, but its oxalates block much of it from being absorbed, so legumes, ragi and til are more reliable everyday iron sources.

herbs.name: Neem

traditionalUse.text: Called 'the wonder tree' and 'nature's drugstore' in Ayurvedic tradition - every part of the tree (leaves, bark, seed oil) has a long history of therapeutic, dental and household use across the Indian subcontinent, among the most widely used plants in traditional Indian medicine.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Folk/home-remedy use leans heavily topical and external: neem leaf powder dusted on skin, mixed into a paste, or used in a bath, traditionally for various skin complaints. This is traditional practice, not independently verified clinical evidence.
traditionalUse.label: illustration

whatEvidenceShows.text: An honest, Indian-dermatology-specific peer-reviewed review states plainly: 'Although there is no evidence of efficacy, neem is extensively used for medicinal purposes in India,' and that 'the scarcity of human trials has obscured its role in modern medicine.' For most skin conditions neem is traditionally used for - acne, eczema, pruritus, scaly scalp, dermatophytosis, scabies, psoriasis among them - the same review finds only traditional use or preclinical (lab/animal) data, not real clinical trials.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: The few real human trials that do exist are small, old and not treated as settled even by the review that reports them: a single 50-patient 1994 trial (oral neem alongside topical tar and salicylic acid) for psoriasis; a small randomised proof-of-principle study for tungiasis (a skin parasite, using neem and coconut oil); and a 1992 pilot study for scabies (neem and turmeric). None of these are large or recent enough to be treated as confirming neem's effectiveness for these conditions.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Laboratory and animal studies suggest antimicrobial, antifungal and anticancer activity (including against drug-resistant bacteria and several cancer cell lines), and a small study of HIV-positive volunteers found an extract increased CD4+ cell counts. These are early-stage or preclinical findings only - a major US cancer centre's own page states plainly there are no human studies showing neem to be an effective cancer treatment, and this card does not treat any of these as an established human benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: For oral hygiene, early research is mixed: a neem leaf gel applied to teeth and gums was linked to reduced plaque in one study, but a separate 2-week neem mouth-rinse trial did not reduce plaque or gingivitis.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Neem leaf, bark and seed oil are all plant parts - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there. Given this card's cautions below, topical (on-skin or dental) use has the better evidence and the lower-severity risk profile compared with swallowing neem oil or seed, which carries the most serious documented risks.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules and standardised leaf-powder products are available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Taking neem oil or neem seed by mouth is rated 'Likely Unsafe' for children - this is this card's single most important caution. Serious side effects in infants and small children can happen within hours of swallowing neem oil, including vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, blood disorders, seizures, coma and brain disorders. This is independently corroborated by two further sources, including a peer-reviewed dermatology review that states oral neem is contraindicated in children under 12 and reports documented child deaths from neem oil ingestion.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding: neem oil and bark taken by mouth are rated 'Likely Unsafe' in pregnancy and can cause miscarriage. A peer-reviewed dermatology review independently states oral neem is contraindicated in both pregnancy and lactation.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May harm sperm - avoid when trying to conceive. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here, not independently cross-confirmed by this card's other sources.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May activate the immune system - a caution for autoimmune conditions (such as multiple sclerosis, lupus or rheumatoid arthritis), where it could worsen symptoms, and for organ-transplant recipients, where it could reduce the effectiveness of anti-rejection (immunosuppressant) medicines (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate and corticosteroids named). Both cautions are sourced to one clinical-reference site here; a second source separately found neem extract inhibits several liver enzymes (CYP3A4/5, 2C8, 2C9) that many medicines rely on, in laboratory testing, though its own clinical relevance 'is not known.'
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood sugar - combined with diabetes medicines (insulin, glimepiride, glipizide and pioglitazone named) this could cause dangerously low blood sugar. Anyone with diabetes should talk to their doctor before trying neem and monitor blood sugar closely if they do. The blood-sugar-lowering direction itself is corroborated by a second source's own separate finding of improved glycaemic control in one small metabolic-syndrome study; the specific diabetes-drug interaction caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May reduce lithium clearance (acting somewhat like a diuretic), which could raise lithium to harmful levels in anyone taking it for a mood disorder - a dose adjustment may be needed. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Large doses or long-term oral use are rated 'Possibly Unsafe' and might harm the kidneys and liver - this is a different, broader caution from the acute child-poisoning risk above, and applies to adults too.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Topical use is not automatically risk-free either, worth knowing specifically for a skin-and-hair-focused herb: allergic contact dermatitis to neem oil has been reported (including on the scalp and face when used for hair loss), chewing neem twigs has caused lip leukoderma (a patchy loss of skin pigment) in a case series, and one case report describes neem oil applied to blisters triggering a flare of an existing autoimmune blistering skin condition (bullous pemphigoid). A peer-reviewed review states plainly that 'the exact compounds and the mechanisms of cutaneous adverse effects remain unclear.'
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Freshness and sourcing matter: neem twigs (sometimes chewed as a traditional toothbrush) are often contaminated with fungi within about 2 weeks of harvest, and home-remedy preparations more broadly can carry a fungal/aflatoxin contamination risk - a reason to avoid chewing twigs and to buy packaged products from a reputable brand rather than assuming any neem preparation is automatically safe.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May interfere with blood sugar control; stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery and tell the surgical team. This specific surgery caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here, not independently confirmed by every other source checked for this card.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never give neem oil or neem seed by mouth to a child, in any amount - this is the clearest, highest-stakes rule in this entire card. Serious poisoning in infants and small children can happen within hours, and child deaths from neem oil ingestion are documented.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Seek emergency medical care immediately if a child or adult swallows neem oil or seed and develops vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, or any altered consciousness - do not wait to see if it passes.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Stop using neem on the skin and see a doctor if you notice a rash, blistering, significant redness or a worsening skin reaction after topical use.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - talk to a doctor before using neem (oral or topical) if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive, have an autoimmune condition, take lithium, have diabetes, take immunosuppressant medicine or have had an organ transplant, or have surgery scheduled.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are genuinely not equivalent in risk for this herb specifically, more so than for most others in this project: topical/dental use has the evidence and safety profile described above, while swallowing neem oil or seed carries this card's most serious documented risk (see cautions and redFlags) - the form matters here as much as the dose.

preparationForms.note: Applied to skin, e.g. for traditional skin complaints - not risk-free either (see this card's own cautions on contact dermatitis), but a lower-severity route than swallowing neem oil or seed.
Standardised leaf-powder products and capsules are available; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
The form carrying this card's most serious documented risk - never given to children, and this card does not describe a safe way to use this form at home.

herbs.name: Guggul

traditionalUse.text: A yellowish gum resin (oleo-gum-resin) tapped from the bark of a small, thorny tree native to India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Ayurvedic medicine has used it for centuries to treat arthritis, obesity, skin disorders and high cholesterol, and a standardised extract is approved for marketing in India as a cholesterol-lowering medicine.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Unlike some other herbs this project has checked, this is not a mix-up between two different plants: the scientific literature genuinely uses two botanical names for this same tree - Commiphora mukul and Commiphora wightii (and, in older texts, Balsamodendrum mukul and Balsamodendrum wightii) - reflecting a taxonomic naming change over time, not two different herbs being confused with each other.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: The purified resin on its own (sometimes called Shuddha Guggulu) is one traditional form, but guggul is also very often combined with many other herbs in classical Ayurvedic tablet formulations, such as Yograj Guggulu - a detail that matters for the vegan check below.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Cholesterol is this herb's best-known researched use, and the evidence is genuinely split rather than one-sided - this card shows both sides rather than picking one. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 7 randomised trials (380 participants, mostly standardised guggul/guggulipid extracts, about 12 weeks average) and found an average fall in total cholesterol of about 16.8 mg/dL and in LDL ("bad") cholesterol of about 18.8 mg/dL, with a small rise in HDL ("good") cholesterol and only minor side effects reported overall.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Worth knowing when reading that same review: its own data is shakier than its summary conclusion suggests. The 7 pooled trials showed high variability (statistically, I-squared of 75%, right at the review's own cut-off for trusting a pooled result), and the authors state one single older trial "strongly influenced" the overall effect - with most of the trials run in Western populations, by the review's own count, apart from two exceptions. The review still concludes guggul is "moderately effective," which reads more confident than this underlying unevenness fully supports - a pattern this project has flagged before in other sources' summaries.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Set directly against that pooled finding: a rigorous 2003 US trial (103 adults with high cholesterol, eating their usual Western diet, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 8 weeks) found guggulipid did NOT lower LDL cholesterol - LDL actually rose by 4 to 5% in the guggulipid groups, against a 5% fall on placebo - with no significant change in total cholesterol, HDL or triglycerides either. Six of the guggulipid-treated participants also developed a hypersensitivity skin rash, versus none on placebo. The authors concluded guggulipid "did not appear to improve" cholesterol over the short term in this population and might even raise LDL.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Clinical-reference sources reflect this same unresolved split rather than settling it: a US consumer medical reference rates the cholesterol evidence "insufficient... inconsistent," noting guggul may lower cholesterol for people eating an Indian-style diet but not for people eating a Western diet, while an older nutrition encyclopedia describes early Indian studies as promising but "limited in scope," making their results "unreliable." This card does not present guggul as a settled or reliable way to lower cholesterol.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Acne is the other traditionally and clinically explored use. A small 1994 Indian trial (20 patients with nodulocystic acne, 3 months) found oral gugulipid reduced inflammatory lesions about as well as the antibiotic tetracycline (68% versus 65% reduction, not a statistically significant difference), with people who had oily skin responding particularly well.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: But sources disagree on how much weight that single small, old trial should carry: a US consumer reference rates acne "Possibly Effective" largely on the strength of it, while a cancer-centre clinical database's own review states plainly that "evidence is lacking to support this claim for guggul alone." This card treats acne as a genuinely open question, not a confirmed benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: For weight loss, most research suggests guggul does not meaningfully reduce body weight in people who are overweight or obese - rated "Possibly Ineffective" by a US consumer medical reference. Early, small studies hint at possible pain improvement in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, but the evidence here is rated insufficient to draw a conclusion either way.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: The gum resin itself, and the purified resin (Shuddha Guggulu), are plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Standardised extract (guggulipid) capsules, dosed by guggulsterone content (commonly 2.5 to 3.5%), are the form used in most of the human trials cited above. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: A genuine vegan-specific check worth making, the same way this project flags gelatin capsules: classical multi-herb Ayurvedic tablet formulations that include guggul, such as Yograj Guggulu, are not vegan as traditionally made - ghee is a direct ingredient in that recipe, and honey or buttermilk is the traditional way the tablets are taken. Choosing a plain guggul or guggulipid extract product, and checking the full ingredient label on any combination "guggulu" product, is the safer route for staying vegan.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

cautions.text: Likely unsafe in pregnancy - it may stimulate the uterus and menstrual flow, so a US consumer medical reference rates it "Likely Unsafe" in pregnancy, and an older nutrition encyclopedia independently makes the same point ("probably unsafe for pregnant women"). Not enough is known about breastfeeding safety either, so the same sources advise avoiding it.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May raise thyroid hormone activity. A cancer-centre clinical database lists guggul as able to elevate TSH, T3 and T4 on lab tests, an academic nutrition textbook describes Commiphora mukul as showing "strong thyroid stimulatory action" in animal research, and a consumer medical reference advises using guggul only under a doctor's supervision if you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine. See this project's own Thyroid health topic for the related caution.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May act like oestrogen in the body - avoid with breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis or uterine fibroids, and avoid combining it with oestrogen-containing medicines or birth control pills.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May slow blood clotting - use caution with a bleeding disorder, and avoid combining with blood-thinning medicines (aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, heparin and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are named) without medical advice. Stop taking guggul at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May change how the liver breaks down several medicines (it can affect the CYP3A4 liver enzyme), which may make some medicines less effective. Examples named across sources include some statins (lovastatin, atorvastatin), some antifungal and allergy medicines, and tamoxifen - one source states plainly not to combine guggul with tamoxifen. Anyone on regular prescription medicine should check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Skin hypersensitivity (an allergic-type rash or itching) is a real, documented reaction - seen in a formal clinical trial (6 of 67 people taking guggulipid, versus none on placebo) and in contact-dermatitis case reports linked to topical slimming or anti-cellulite creams containing guggul.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: A small number of case reports describe raised liver enzymes or liver injury linked to guggul-containing products, but this project treats the signal as real but unproven, not a confirmed guggul-specific risk - weaker and more confounded than the liver-injury finding this project has documented for Giloy. The reported cases involved combination products (one alongside red yeast rice, one alongside usnic acid and green tea), and the reviewing source itself says it is unclear how much guggul, versus the other ingredients, was responsible. Separately, a 2020 US government toxicology study found no dose-related organ damage in a 3-month animal study, though this is animal data, not proof of human safety.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Milder, more common side effects include stomach upset, headache, nausea, vomiting, loose stools or diarrhoea, belching and hiccups - more likely at higher doses (around 6000 mg/day in the sources reviewed).
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine, talk to your doctor before trying guggul, and ask about monitoring thyroid function with blood tests if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take blood-thinning medicine, have a bleeding disorder, have surgery scheduled, take tamoxifen or another hormone-sensitive-cancer medicine, or take any regular prescription medicine, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using guggul.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Stop taking guggul and see a doctor if you notice a widespread rash or itching, yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusually dark urine, or persistent nausea - these need medical attention, not waiting to see if they pass.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - avoid guggul if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and check with a doctor if you are trying to conceive or have a hormone-sensitive condition.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - the human trials behind this card's cholesterol and acne findings used a standardised guggulipid extract dosed by guggulsterone content, not raw resin or a multi-herb tablet. Classical combination tablets such as Yograj Guggulu also raise a separate, vegan-specific issue: ghee is a direct ingredient in that recipe, so check labels rather than assuming any product called "guggul" or "guggulu" is plant-only.

preparationForms.note: Raw or purified resin, a traditional Ayurvedic form - naturally vegan, but not the form used in the clinical trials cited above.

Standardised extract dosed by guggulsterone content (commonly 2.5-3.5%). The Western cholesterol trial used 1000-2000 mg guggulipid three times daily; the acne trial used a dose giving 25 mg guggulsterone twice daily. Check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.

preparationForms.form: Tablet (classical multi-herb formulation, e.g. Yograj Guggulu)
preparationForms.note: Combines guggul resin with many other herbs; ghee is a direct ingredient in this classical recipe, and honey or buttermilk is the traditional way to take it - not vegan as traditionally made. Choose a plain guggul/guggulipid product instead to stay vegan, and check the full label.
